marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q001.takeaway: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the duodenum/pancreas and does not contribute to the stomach’s arterial supply.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q001.displayText:
The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the duodenum/pancreas and does not contribute to the stomach’s arterial supply.

The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery does not contribute to the blood supply of the stomach. It is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. It supplies the duodenum (second and third parts) and the pancreas (head and uncinate process).

The arterial supply of the stomach is contributed exclusively by the coeliac trunk through its branches: left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature; splenic artery gives short gastric arteries to the fundus and the left gastroepiploic artery to the greater curvature; common hepatic artery gives the right gastric artery to the lesser curvature and the gastroduodenal artery, from which the right gastroepiploic artery supplies the greater curvature.

Clinical note: The presence of an abnormal, tortuous artery in the submucosa of the lesser curvature is called a Dieulafoy's lesion. As it is superficial, it is more vulnerable to rupture causing significant haemorrhage.
emphasis: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the duodenum/pancreas and does not contribute to the stomach’s arterial supply

rationales.a: Common hepatic branches, including right gastric/gastroduodenal routes, supply stomach.
rationales.b: Splenic artery gives short gastric and left gastroepiploic branches to stomach.
rationales.c: Gastroduodenal artery gives right gastroepiploic and related gastric branches.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q002.takeaway: Common hepatic artery interruption can compromise right gastric and right gastroepiploic routes through hepatic/gastroduodenal branches.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q002.displayText:
Common hepatic artery interruption can compromise right gastric and right gastroepiploic routes through hepatic/gastroduodenal branches.

Ligation of the common hepatic artery will cause impairment in the blood supply through its branches, i.e. the right gastric artery and right gastroepiploic artery.

The arterial supply of the stomach is contributed exclusively by branches of the coeliac trunk: the left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature; the splenic artery gives short gastric arteries to the fundus and the left gastroepiploic artery to the greater curvature; and the common hepatic artery gives the right gastric artery and the gastroduodenal artery, from which the right gastroepiploic artery arises.
emphasis: Common hepatic artery interruption can compromise right gastric and right gastroepiploic routes through hepatic/gastroduodenal branches

rationales.b: Left gastric artery arises directly from celiac trunk and is not dependent on common hepatic.
rationales.c: Short gastric arteries arise from splenic artery and are not dependent on common hepatic.
rationales.d: Short gastric flow is from splenic artery; this pair does not match the common hepatic branches.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q003.takeaway: The criminal nerve of Grassi is a posterior vagal branch supplying the fundus that may be missed during vagotomy.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q003.displayText:
The criminal nerve of Grassi is a posterior vagal branch supplying the fundus that may be missed during vagotomy.

The posterior vagus nerve gives rise to the criminal nerve of Grassi.

This nerve supplies the cardia and fundus of the stomach. It is called a criminal nerve because it is often missed during a vagotomy procedure and can result in recurrent peptic ulcer disease.

The sympathetic supply arises from T5-T12 spinal segments and reaches the stomach through the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves and the coeliac plexus. It causes vasoconstriction, constriction of the pyloric sphincter with inhibition of gastric motility, and carries visceral pain sensations.

The parasympathetic supply arises from the right and left vagus nerves. The anterior vagal trunk is formed from the left vagus nerve, whereas the posterior vagal trunk is formed from the right vagus nerve. Parasympathetic actions include secretomotor supply to gastric glands, motor supply to gastric musculature, relaxation of the pyloric sphincter with promotion of gastric emptying, and carriage of sensations such as fullness, nausea, and probably pain.
emphasis: The criminal nerve of Grassi is a posterior vagal branch supplying the fundus that may be missed during vagotomy

rationales.b: The anterior vagus gives anterior gastric/Latarjet branches, not the criminal posterior fundic branch.
rationales.c: Greater splanchnic carries sympathetic fibers and does not give the nerve of Grassi.
rationales.d: Lesser splanchnic is also sympathetic and unrelated to vagal fundic branches.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q004.takeaway: The prepyloric vein of Mayo drains into the right gastric vein and marks the pyloric region.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q004.displayText:
The prepyloric vein of Mayo drains into the right gastric vein and marks the pyloric region.

The right gastric vein receives the prepyloric vein of Mayo.

The prepyloric vein serves as a guidepost for surgeons to identify the pylorus of the stomach.

The common pattern of venous drainage is: right gastric vein to portal vein; left gastric vein to portal vein; right gastroepiploic vein to superior mesenteric vein; left gastroepiploic vein to splenic vein; short gastric veins to splenic vein.
emphasis: The prepyloric vein of Mayo drains into the right gastric vein and marks the pyloric region

rationales.a: Right gastroepiploic vein drains the greater curvature.
rationales.b: Left gastroepiploic vein drains the left greater curvature toward splenic vein.
rationales.c: Left gastric vein drains the lesser curvature proximally, not the prepyloric vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q005.takeaway: Gastric lymph passes through celiac nodes to the intestinal lymph trunk, then cisterna chyli and thoracic duct.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q005.displayText:
Gastric lymph passes through celiac nodes to the intestinal lymph trunk, then cisterna chyli and thoracic duct.

Among the given options, the intestinal lymph trunk is the last structure to drain lymphatics from the stomach.

The intestinal lymph trunk is a major lymphatic channel in the abdomen. It receives lymphatics from the pre-aortic group of lymph nodes such as coeliac nodes, superior mesenteric nodes, and inferior mesenteric nodes. The intestinal lymph trunk finally drains into the cisterna chyli.

The lymphatic drainage of the stomach can be divided into four zones as shown in the source figure.
emphasis: Gastric lymph passes through celiac nodes to the intestinal lymph trunk, then cisterna chyli and thoracic duct

rationales.a: Celiac nodes are an intermediate drainage station, not the final collecting channel.
rationales.c: Para-aortic nodes are not the final main trunk for gastric lymph.
rationales.d: Lumbar lymph trunks drain lower limbs/posterior abdominal wall; intestinal trunk collects gut lymph.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q006.takeaway: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anterior to the third part of the duodenum and can compress it in SMA syndrome.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q006.displayText:
The superior mesenteric artery crosses anterior to the third part of the duodenum and can compress it in SMA syndrome.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of superior mesenteric artery syndrome or Wilkie syndrome. In this condition, the third part of the duodenum is compressed by the superior mesenteric artery, causing bowel obstruction.

The mid-portion of the third part of the duodenum lies in the angle between the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly and the abdominal aorta posteriorly.
emphasis: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anterior to the third part of the duodenum and can compress it in SMA syndrome

rationales.a: IVC lies posterior to the duodenum and does not normally compress it from the anterior side.
rationales.b: Right gonadal vessels are small and do not form the characteristic compression.
rationales.d: Aorta lies posterior to the third duodenal part; the compressing vessel is SMA anteriorly.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q007.takeaway: The splenic artery does not supply the duodenum; the first jejunal branch from SMA contributes to its fourth part.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q007.displayText:
The splenic artery does not supply the duodenum; the first jejunal branch from SMA contributes to its fourth part.

The splenic artery does not supply the duodenum.

The major vessels supplying the duodenum are the gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, and the superior mesenteric artery, an anterior branch of the abdominal aorta.

Branches of the gastroduodenal artery supplying the first and second parts of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas include the posterior and anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, supraduodenal artery, retroduodenal arteries, and pancreatic branches. The first and second parts also receive minor supply from the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries.

Branches of the superior mesenteric artery supplying the second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum and the head and uncinate process include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (anterior and posterior branches) and the first jejunal artery, which supplies the fourth part.
emphasis: The splenic artery does not supply the duodenum; the first jejunal branch from SMA contributes to its fourth part

rationales.a: Common hepatic branches contribute to the gastroduodenal arcade supplying duodenum.
rationales.b: Right gastric artery may supply proximal duodenum through gastric/duodenal branches in the source scheme.
rationales.c: The first jejunal artery is a branch of the SMA that supplies the fourth duodenal part, so a jejunal branch can contribute; the splenic artery does not supply duodenum.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q008.takeaway: Plicae circulares are most prominent in jejunum and increase absorptive surface area.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q008.displayText:
Plicae circulares are most prominent in jejunum and increase absorptive surface area.

The image shows plicae circulares, also known as valvulae conniventes. They are more prominent in the jejunum.

Plicae circulares are circular mucosal folds. They frequently branch and stack upon each other, giving the jejunum a characteristic feathery appearance in single-contrast radiography.
emphasis: Plicae circulares are most prominent in jejunum and increase absorptive surface area

rationales.a: Plicae are present in ileum but are less prominent distally.
rationales.c: Duodenum has folds but not the most prominent pattern.
rationales.d: Ascending colon has haustra, not small-intestinal plicae circulares.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q009.takeaway: Meckel diverticulum arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum as a remnant of the vitelline duct.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q009.displayText:
Meckel diverticulum arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum as a remnant of the vitelline duct.

Meckel's diverticulum projects from the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum. It is commonly located 2 feet proximal to the ileocaecal valve.

Peyer's patches are lymphoid aggregates present in the submucosa and are arranged longitudinally along the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
emphasis: Meckel diverticulum arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum as a remnant of the vitelline duct

rationales.a: Peyer patches are lymphoid aggregates on the antimesenteric ileum, not at the mesenteric border as stated.
rationales.b: Meckel diverticulum is in ileum, not jejunum, and is antimesenteric.
rationales.d: Peyer patches are typically ileal and not the antimesenteric jejunal match given.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q010.takeaway: The transverse colon is usually the longest part of the large intestine because of its variable length and mobility.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q010.displayText:
The transverse colon is usually the longest part of the large intestine because of its variable length and mobility.

The transverse colon is the longest part of the large intestine, measuring about 50 cm in length on average. It is intraperitoneal and suspended by the transverse mesocolon.

The source table lists approximate lengths: caecum 6 cm; ascending colon 15-20 cm; transverse colon 50 cm; descending colon 25-30 cm; sigmoid colon 37.5 cm; rectum 15 cm; anal canal 2-5 cm.
emphasis: The transverse colon is usually the longest part of the large intestine because of its variable length and mobility

rationales.b: Descending colon is shorter and relatively fixed.
rationales.c: Ascending colon is shorter than transverse colon.
rationales.d: Sigmoid colon is variable but usually shorter than transverse colon.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q011.takeaway: Appendices epiploicae are usually absent from the caecum; the marked fatty tags are not typically present there.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q011.displayText:
Appendices epiploicae are usually absent from the caecum; the marked fatty tags are not typically present there.

The marked structures are appendices epiploicae and they are usually absent in the caecum.

Appendices epiploicae are small fat-filled peritoneal pouches scattered over the surface of the large intestine. They are very abundant on the surface of the sigmoid colon and tend to be absent from the caecum, rectum, and appendix.
emphasis: Appendices epiploicae are usually absent from the caecum; the marked fatty tags are not typically present there

rationales.a: Sigmoid colon has abundant appendices epiploicae.
rationales.b: Descending colon usually bears appendices epiploicae.
rationales.c: Transverse colon has appendices epiploicae along its surface.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q012.takeaway: The marginal artery at the splenic flexure links left colic from IMA with middle colic from SMA.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q012.displayText:
The marginal artery at the splenic flexure links left colic from IMA with middle colic from SMA.

The middle and left colic arteries contribute to the formation of the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is a watershed area of the colon that is more prone to ischemia.

The marginal artery of Drummond runs in the mesentery along the inner margin of the colon. It is formed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery (middle colic, right colic, ileocolic) and branches of the inferior mesenteric artery (left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal).

When ischemia occurs at Griffith's point, blood supply can be augmented by the inner arterial arc of Riolan, which connects the main trunk of the middle colic artery with the ascending branch of the left colic artery.

Clinical note: Sudeck's point is another watershed area at the rectosigmoid junction. The sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery at this site.
emphasis: The marginal artery at the splenic flexure links left colic from IMA with middle colic from SMA

rationales.a: Right colic does not join left colic as the main flexural watershed supply.
rationales.b: Ileocolic supplies terminal ileum/cecum and is not the principal splenic-flexure contributor.
rationales.d: Sigmoid arteries supply distal descending/sigmoid colon, not the middle-colic connection at flexure.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q013.takeaway: The most common appendix position is retrocaecal (label 2 in the source image), consistent with a positive psoas sign.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q013.displayText:
The most common appendix position is retrocaecal (label 2 in the source image), consistent with a positive psoas sign.

The clinical scenario points towards appendicitis and the most common position of the appendix is retrocaecal. In the numbered question image, this is position 2. This is because the appendix develops during the descent of the colon in embryonic life.

The base of the appendix is fixed and, depending on the direction of its tip, the positions include retrocaecal, pelvic, paracolic, subcaecal, pre-ileal, post-ileal, and promonteric.

Clinical note: The ilio-psoas sign is pain elicited on extension of the hip and is seen in retrocaecal appendicitis. The obturator sign is pain elicited on internal rotation of the hip and is seen in pelvic appendicitis.
emphasis: The most common appendix position is retrocaecal (label 2 in the source image), consistent with a positive psoas sign

rationales.a: Label 1 is not the retrocaecal position identified in the source diagram.
rationales.c: Label 3 represents another variant direction, not the common retrocaecal orientation.
rationales.d: Label 4 is not the most frequent appendix position.

marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q014.takeaway: The middle rectal artery travels in the lateral rectal ligament with connective tissue and autonomic fibers.
marrow__ANAT_CH49_Q014.displayText:
The middle rectal artery travels in the lateral rectal ligament with connective tissue and autonomic fibers.

The middle rectal artery is a content of the lateral rectal ligament.

The condensation of the endopelvic fascia that surrounds the middle rectal vessels is referred to as the lateral rectal ligament. Branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus also enter the rectum through this ligament.
emphasis: The middle rectal artery travels in the lateral rectal ligament with connective tissue and autonomic fibers

rationales.a: Superior rectal artery descends in the mesorectum from the IMA, not lateral ligament as the keyed structure.
rationales.b: Left superior rectal artery is part of the mesorectal vascular pedicle.
rationales.d: Inferior rectal artery supplies anal canal/perineum from internal pudendal artery.
